name: Austin
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Austin, TX | Genstone
metaDescription: Austin investor renovations scoped around HOME-rule lot options, tree permits, Balcones clay vs. limestone, and Development Services review, priced pre-offer.
intro: Renovating in Austin means working in a city that changed its own rules underneath investors. The HOME initiative opened most single-family lots to additional units, the tree ordinance can decide where an addition goes, and the Development Services Department reviews more residential work than many Texas cities do. Meanwhile the housing itself splits along the Balcones Fault: older bungalows and ranches east of MoPac sit on shifting Blackland clay, while homes in the west and southwest sit on shallow limestone. After the run-up and pullback in prices over the last several years, the margin on an Austin deal depends on getting the scope right the first time. Genstone Construction coordinates vetted, licensed contractors across Austin for investors, lenders and servicers, managed by our estimators and field managers from Romeoville, Illinois. A free Pre-Offer Rehab Review tells you what the house needs and whether the ARV supports it, before your earnest money is at risk.
housingStock:
Austin's older housing is a thin layer compared with its newer growth, which is exactly why investors compete so hard for it.

The prewar core includes Hyde Park, North University, Clarksville, Travis Heights, Bouldin Creek and parts of East Austin. Hyde Park holds Victorian and Craftsman houses from the 1890s through the 1930s, many with original long-leaf pine floors, tall windows and wood siding. Travis Heights and Bouldin Creek mix bungalows with 1930s and 1940s cottages on hilly, tree-covered lots. East Austin neighborhoods like Holly, Govalle, Rosewood and Chestnut were built with small frame houses on pier-and-beam foundations, and a large share of those lots have already been rebuilt with modern infill.

The postwar ring is where most investor renovation happens. Crestview, Brentwood, Allandale, Windsor Park, Highland and Cherrywood filled in from the late 1940s through the 1960s with modest ranches, many with wood or asbestos-cement siding, original single-pane windows, small panels, galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains. Some sit on pier-and-beam, many on early slabs. These houses sit close to central employment and transit, so buyers and tenants want them even when the floor plans feel small.

The 1970s and 1980s brought tract neighborhoods in Dove Springs, Montopolis, the Rundberg area, North Lamar and much of South Austin, along with the city's distinctive stock of side-by-side duplexes built on single lots. Those homes bring era-specific issues: aluminum branch wiring in some, polybutylene supply lines in some, composite siding, original HVAC and flat or low-slope additions. Ground conditions change sharply across town. East of the fault, clay heaves and shrinks with Austin's wet-dry cycles. West of it, limestone is stable but makes trenching for plumbing slow and expensive, and hillside lots in Travis Heights and the southwest add retaining walls and drainage to the list.

commonIssues.title: Clay movement east of MoPac
commonIssues.body: Neighborhoods on the Blackland clay east of the Balcones Fault, including Windsor Park, Cherrywood, Montopolis and much of East Austin, see seasonal foundation movement as soils swell during wet springs and shrink in long droughts. Slabs crack and pier-and-beam floors slope. On these houses we budget for a foundation evaluation and leveling or piers before finish work, and we fix gutters and grading so the repair is not undone by roof runoff.

commonIssues.title: Protected trees and lot constraints
commonIssues.body: Austin's tree ordinance protects larger trees and gives heritage trees additional protection, and the critical root zone around them limits where you can dig, pour or build. That affects sewer line replacements, additions, new driveways and even foundation work on mature central lots. We check tree locations early, plan trenching routes and footprints around them, and allow for arborist input where the city requires it, so the scope does not stall at plan review.

commonIssues.title: Asbestos siding and old materials
commonIssues.body: Many postwar Austin ranches were clad in asbestos-cement shingle siding, and interiors from the same era often hold asbestos in floor tile, mastic, ceiling texture or duct wrap. Nearly all pre-1978 houses also carry lead paint. Removal or disturbance requires testing and, where materials are present, licensed abatement or lead-safe practices. We include testing in scoping so you are not surprised when a wall or floor is opened.

commonIssues.title: Old plumbing under slabs and in rock
commonIssues.body: Galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains are common in Crestview, Brentwood and Allandale ranches, and clay movement on the east side cracks them further. In west and southwest Austin, replacing a drain line can mean cutting through limestone, which changes the method and the price. A camera inspection before purchase tells us whether you need a spot repair, a reroute or full replacement, and how hard the ground will be.

commonIssues.title: Unpermitted additions and conversions
commonIssues.body: Decades of informal improvements left many Austin houses with enclosed garages, rear additions, converted carports and backyard structures that were never permitted. With HOME rules allowing more units on a lot, some investors want to legalize them as dwellings. That can work, but the structure must meet current code, and setbacks, impervious cover limits and tree protections still apply. We evaluate each structure and price legalization, repair or removal.

investorMarket:
Austin investors are splitting into two camps: those who renovate the house and those who renovate the lot.

In central neighborhoods like Hyde Park, Travis Heights, Bouldin Creek, Crestview, Brentwood and Allandale, flips still work when the house has character or a good postwar layout and the buyer wants to live there rather than redevelop. These buyers pay for updated kitchens and baths, fully replaced systems and preserved details, and they compare your house against new infill nearby. Historic districts and the city's residential design standards limit how much you can expand some of these homes.

Under the HOME initiative, many investors now look at central and east lots for added units: keeping the existing house, renovating it, and adding a second or third dwelling behind it. That turns a flip into a small development project, with very different permitting, utility and tree questions.

Farther out, Dove Springs, Montopolis, St. Johns, the Rundberg corridor and parts of Pflugerville and Manor suit buy-and-hold and BRRRR strategies. Purchase prices are lower, rent demand is supported by the region's tech, health care and service employers, and scopes center on systems, roofs and durable interiors. Austin's stock of 1980s duplexes also attracts small multifamily investors, especially in South and North Central Austin. Because prices corrected after their peak, these strategies depend on careful rehab budgeting rather than appreciation, and the Pre-Offer Rehab Review is built for that.
permits:
Residential permits inside the city are issued by the City of Austin Development Services Department. Structural work, foundation repair, additions, new or relocated plumbing and electrical, HVAC replacement, re-roofing and most window changes that alter openings require permits and inspections, and trade permits must be pulled by contractors licensed through the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners or the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation.

Several Austin-specific rules affect investor scopes. The tree ordinance requires review for work within the critical root zone of protected and heritage trees. Central neighborhoods fall under residential design and compatibility standards that limit building size and form. The HOME initiative now allows additional units on most single-family lots, but each new unit triggers its own review for setbacks, impervious cover, utilities and fire access. Properties in local historic districts, such as Hyde Park and Travis Heights–Fairview Park, need Historic Landmark Commission or staff review for exterior changes. At sale, Austin Energy's Energy Conservation Audit and Disclosure ordinance requires an energy audit for many older homes in its service area, which flippers should plan for. Addresses outside city limits, including Pflugerville, Round Rock and unincorporated Travis County, fall under their own building offices.
climate:
Austin's weather swings between long, dry heat and sudden, heavy rain, and both shape a renovation. Summer heat slows roofing, exterior painting and concrete work, and attic work is best done early in the day. Drought dries clay soils east of the fault and accelerates foundation movement.

When rain comes, it can come hard. Central Texas sits in Flash Flood Alley, and creeks like Shoal, Onion, Williamson and Walnut have flooded neighborhoods along their banks, so flood history and drainage deserve a look on any creekside house. Spring brings hail that can replace roofs across whole neighborhoods. Winter is usually mild, but Winter Storm Uri in 2021 burst pipes across the city, and the 2023 ice storm brought down limbs from mature trees onto roofs and power lines. We plan freeze protection, tree trimming over roofs and roof scheduling around those patterns.

faqs.q: Do you work in Round Rock, Pflugerville and other Austin suburbs?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate licensed contractors across the Austin metro, including Round Rock, Pflugerville, Cedar Park, Leander, Georgetown, Manor, Kyle and Buda. Each city runs its own building department, and many suburban subdivisions have homeowners associations with exterior rules. Unincorporated areas fall under Travis or Williamson County. We confirm jurisdiction and any HOA restrictions for each address before scoping, so the permit plan matches the property.

faqs.q: Can I add a unit to my Austin property under HOME?
faqs.a: Many single-family lots in Austin can now hold additional units under the HOME initiative, but feasibility depends on lot size, setbacks, impervious cover, trees, utility capacity and fire access. A renovation of the existing house plus a new unit behind it is a common approach. We can price the renovation side and help you understand which site constraints will drive the design, so you can bring in an architect with realistic expectations.

faqs.q: What is the ECAD requirement for selling an Austin flip?
faqs.a: Austin Energy's Energy Conservation Audit and Disclosure ordinance requires sellers of many older homes in its service area to have an energy audit performed and disclosed to buyers. For a flip, it makes sense to complete the renovation's efficiency work, such as attic insulation, duct sealing and new HVAC, before the audit so the results reflect the improvements. We schedule that work so the audit can happen before listing.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay anything before work starts?
faqs.a: No. Genstone takes no upfront payment on Austin projects. Draws are released against completed, photographed stages of work, and the final payment is due only after completion and your approval. Dumpster and debris costs are built into the estimate from the beginning. Our work carries a one-year workmanship warranty that excludes tenant damage and normal wear, and lien waivers and contractor compliance records are kept for your lender, buyer or partners.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Austin, TX | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Austin fix and flip renovations for Crestview, Allandale and Travis Heights buyers: midcentury layouts, ECAD-ready efficiency, tree-aware plumbing and permits.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Austin
fix-flip.intro: An Austin flip lives or dies on whether the buyer sees a home or a teardown. In Crestview, Brentwood and Allandale, buyers want a midcentury ranch with a smarter layout, real insulation and new systems, close to the Domain and downtown without paying new-construction prices. In Travis Heights and Hyde Park, they want an older house that still feels original. Everywhere in the city, buyers have new infill to compare against, so a half-finished flip stands out for the wrong reasons. Genstone builds Austin flip scopes around those buyers and around the city's rules: energy audits at sale, tree protections, design standards and historic review. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work and stress-tests your ARV before you commit, and one field manager coordinates licensed local contractors from demolition through final inspection.

sections.h2: Midcentury ranches in Crestview, Brentwood and Allandale
sections.body:
The bread-and-butter Austin flip is a 1950s or 1960s ranch north of central Austin. These houses tend to have small, closed kitchens, a single bath or a bath and a half, low ceilings, original single-pane windows, thin attic insulation and wood or asbestos-cement siding. Buyers want an open kitchen and living area, a second full bath or a much better primary bath, efficient windows and HVAC, and a clean modern exterior.

We scope these houses carefully because the wall you want to remove may carry the roof, and the bath you want to add needs a drain route that may run under a slab or through a crawlspace. Asbestos siding and floor tile need testing and abatement before demolition. On the efficiency side, we plan attic insulation, duct sealing or replacement, new windows and right-sized HVAC early, because Austin Energy's audit at sale will show buyers how the house performs. Finishes should match the comps on your street: clean, durable materials with a few design choices that photograph well, rather than high-end selections that the appraisal will not support.

sections.h2: Older homes in Hyde Park, Travis Heights and Bouldin
sections.body:
In Austin's prewar neighborhoods, buyers pay for original details and expect everything behind the walls to be new. A Hyde Park bungalow or Victorian usually needs foundation leveling, rewiring to remove old circuits, new plumbing, central HVAC routed through the attic or crawlspace and restoration of wood siding, windows and porches. Long-leaf pine floors should be refinished rather than covered if they can be saved.

Rules matter more here than elsewhere. Hyde Park and Travis Heights–Fairview Park are local historic districts, so exterior changes such as window replacement, siding changes, porch alterations and additions need review. The city's residential design and compatibility standards limit how large an addition can be and how it relates to neighbors. Mature trees on these lots can determine where a new sewer line or addition can go. We check all of this during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, then build a scope that stays inside the rules, so you are not redesigning in the middle of the project while interest accrues.

sections.h2: Carrying costs, reviews and the Austin calendar
sections.body:
Austin flips tend to lose time in review rather than in construction. Work that needs only trade permits can move quickly, but anything involving structural changes, additions, tree root zones or historic districts takes longer. We separate the scope into what can start immediately and what needs review, so interior demolition, abatement and rough-in work proceed while approvals are pending.

Weather and season matter too. Summer heat slows roofing and exterior paint, and spring hail can delay roof replacements as crews get booked. We plan the ECAD energy audit after the efficiency work is done, so the report helps rather than hurts your listing. Draws are tied to completed work, and milestone photos let you track progress and keep lenders informed without visiting the site. With prices having come off their peak, disciplined scope and schedule are where Austin flip margins come from now. We would rather show you a tight, realistic plan before closing than discover a review delay halfway through demolition.

faqs.q: Should I flip an Austin house or sell it as a lot?
faqs.a: That depends on the house, the lot and the neighborhood. In some central and east Austin locations, the land is worth more than the house to a builder, especially under HOME rules allowing added units. In others, a well-renovated house sells for more than the lot alone. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the renovation so you can compare the flip outcome against a land sale before you decide.

faqs.q: How do protected trees affect a flip?
faqs.a: If a protected or heritage tree's root zone overlaps the area where you need to trench a sewer line, add a room, pour a driveway or repair a foundation, the work may need review and special methods. We check tree locations during scoping and plan routes and footprints to avoid conflicts, which keeps the permit process from stalling and protects a feature buyers often value.

faqs.q: Do I need an energy audit before I list?
faqs.a: Many older homes in Austin Energy's service area require an Energy Conservation Audit and Disclosure at sale. We recommend doing the efficiency work first, such as insulation, duct sealing, windows and HVAC, then scheduling the audit so it reflects the renovated house. That way the disclosure supports your price instead of raising questions. Buyers comparing your ranch against new infill often read the audit closely.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Austin, TX | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: Austin BRRRR rehabs in Dove Springs, Montopolis and St. Johns: systems-first scopes that appraise on refinance, tenant-proof finishes and HOME-unit options.
brrrr.intro: BRRRR in Austin has gotten harder and more interesting at the same time. Purchase prices in the urban core rarely leave room for a refinance that returns your capital, but neighborhoods like Dove Springs, Montopolis, St. Johns, the Rundberg corridor and parts of Pflugerville still offer houses where a systems-first rehab creates real value. And the HOME initiative gives some investors a second lever: renovate the existing house and add a rentable unit on the same lot. Genstone scopes Austin BRRRR projects to satisfy the refinance appraiser and to hold up to years of tenants. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work and estimates ARV before you buy, and Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans for the refinance if you want one partner across both steps. One field manager coordinates licensed contractors and permits throughout the project.

sections.h2: What moves an Austin refinance appraisal
sections.body:
Austin appraisers lean on recent sales nearby and adjust heavily for condition and functional problems. On the 1970s and 1980s houses that make up much of Dove Springs, St. Johns and the Rundberg area, the items that hurt an appraisal are predictable: original HVAC, aluminum branch wiring in some homes, polybutylene supply lines in some, roof age, foundation movement on clay, and dated kitchens and baths. Addressing the systems first usually does more for the number than upgrading finishes.

We target finishes to what comparable rentals and sales support in each area, which usually means durable vinyl plank, mid-range counters and clean, standard fixtures. Spending more rarely helps an appraisal in these neighborhoods. Square footage matters too, so if a previous owner enclosed a garage or added a room without permits, we discuss whether to legalize it or return it to its original use. Permit records, any foundation reports and roof documentation are organized for the underwriter so questions get answered quickly.

sections.h2: Durable rentals for Austin heat and storms
sections.body:
Austin rentals run their air conditioning hard for much of the year, so HVAC sizing, ductwork condition and attic insulation drive both tenant comfort and service calls. We size equipment to the house, seal or replace leaky ducts in hot attics, add insulation where it is thin and make sure condensate lines drain properly. Efficient systems also help with Austin Energy bills, which tenants notice.

Inside, we choose waterproof vinyl plank, scrubbable paint, solid cabinets and standard fixtures that can be replaced from stock. Outside, we look at gutters, downspouts and grading so roof water drains away from the foundation, which matters on clay east of the fault. After Winter Storm Uri and the 2023 ice storm, we also check for exposed plumbing in exterior walls and attics and trim limbs that hang over the roof. These choices keep turnover costs down and protect the value you will need at the next refinance or sale.

sections.h2: Using HOME rules alongside a BRRRR
sections.body:
Some Austin investors now combine BRRRR with an added unit. The strategy is to buy a house on a lot that can support another dwelling, renovate the main house for rent, then add a second unit behind it or convert an existing structure into a legal unit. Done well, the property produces more rent and may support a stronger refinance. Done poorly, it becomes an expensive, slow development project.

The constraints are real: setbacks, impervious cover limits, tree protections, utility capacity, fire access and the cost of new water and electrical service. We can price the renovation of the existing house and help you understand what the site will allow before you commit. For many investors, the practical path is to renovate and rent the main house first, then plan the second unit once the first refinance is done. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review is a good place to start sorting that out.

faqs.q: Can Genstone Financial refinance my Austin rental?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial is the lending arm of the Genstone Companies, offering DSCR rental loans, fix-and-flip loans, lines of credit and new construction loans. A DSCR loan qualifies on the property's rental income rather than your personal income, which fits many BRRRR investors. You can use any lender you like. We provide the same scope, draw records, permit sign-offs and completion photos either way.

faqs.q: Which Austin neighborhoods work for BRRRR now?
faqs.a: Areas such as Dove Springs, Montopolis, St. Johns, the Rundberg corridor and parts of Pflugerville and Manor tend to offer purchase prices that leave room for a full rehab and a refinance. Central neighborhoods usually do not, unless the deal includes added units. We look at comps, rent levels and scope for each house before you buy, so the strategy matches the numbers.

faqs.q: Do you handle legalizing a garage conversion?
faqs.a: Yes. We evaluate the existing structure for framing, insulation, electrical, plumbing, egress and fire separation, then price the work needed to bring it to code and the permit path with Development Services. Sometimes legalization is straightforward. Sometimes it is cheaper to return the space to a garage. We show you both before you decide, along with how each choice is likely to affect the appraised square footage on your refinance.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Austin, TX | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Austin single-family rental rehabs across Travis and Williamson counties: efficient HVAC, clay-aware drainage, durable finishes and one portfolio standard.
rental-renovation.intro: Austin's single-family rental stock looks different from Houston's or Dallas's. Inside the city, landlords hold 1950s ranches in Windsor Park and Crestview, 1970s and 1980s tract houses in Dove Springs and the Rundberg area, and older homes near the university that rent by the room. Outside it, institutional and individual owners hold large numbers of 2000s and 2010s tract homes in Pflugerville, Round Rock, Hutto, Manor, Kyle and Leander. A rental program that works here has to handle both old housing with real structural and material issues and newer housing where the problems are mostly mechanical and cosmetic. Genstone renovates and turns rental homes for landlords, funds and institutional owners across the Austin metro, with one written standard, one field manager per property and draw documentation built for asset managers.

sections.h2: Old Austin rentals versus suburban tract homes
sections.body:
Our portfolio standard covers the baseline every Austin rental needs: waterproof vinyl plank, one paint family, stock cabinets and fixtures, sealed ductwork, correctly sized HVAC, smart thermostats where owners want them, working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and secure locks. Where the money goes beyond that depends on the age of the house.

On older rentals inside the city, such as the postwar ranches of Windsor Park, Highland and Crestview, scopes often include testing and abating asbestos siding or floor tile, replacing galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains, upgrading small electrical panels and addressing foundation movement on clay soils. On 1970s and 1980s houses in Dove Springs, Montopolis and South Austin, we watch for aluminum branch wiring, polybutylene supply lines in some builds and original HVAC. On newer suburban tract homes, the common items are HVAC equipment reaching the end of its life, water heaters, builder-grade fixtures and flooring, fence repairs and HOA-driven exterior work like paint colors and roof materials. Separating those categories keeps capital plans honest and prevents the portfolio from overspending on simple houses.

sections.h2: Covering Travis, Williamson and Hays counties
sections.body:
Austin portfolios commonly span three counties and a dozen jurisdictions: the City of Austin, Pflugerville, Round Rock, Hutto, Georgetown, Leander, Cedar Park, Manor, Kyle, Buda and unincorporated areas of Travis, Williamson and Hays counties. Each has its own building department and inspection process, and most suburban subdivisions add homeowners associations with rules about exterior colors, fences, roofing and even trash can placement.

Genstone keeps one written scope standard and one documentation format across that spread, while our licensed, insured contractor network performs the work locally. Each property gets a field manager who handles permits, inspections, lien waivers, contractor compliance and HOA requirements. Asset managers see milestone photos and draw requests without traveling. Our estimators also flag capital items beyond a turn, such as foundation work on an older ranch east of the fault, a roof damaged by spring hail, or a house with a recurring drainage problem, so annual budgets reflect actual conditions across the portfolio.

sections.h2: Turns, efficiency and Austin's rental rules
sections.body:
Turns in Austin are a chance to cut operating costs as well as fix wear. Adding attic insulation, sealing ducts and replacing aging HVAC during a vacancy lowers tenant utility bills and reduces summer service calls, which helps retention. Spring turns are the best time for HVAC work before the heat arrives. Fall turns are a good time to check exterior plumbing, hose bibs and attic lines for freeze exposure and to trim tree limbs that could fall on roofs during an ice storm.

Austin Code enforces property maintenance standards on rentals, and properties with repeated violations can be placed in the city's Repeat Offender Program, which brings registration and inspections. Building turns around code-relevant items such as smoke alarms, egress windows, safe electrical, working plumbing and sound stairs and railings keeps properties out of that category. Genstone Field Services also provides occupied maintenance, inspections and code compliance, so one organization can handle both renovation and ongoing upkeep. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the work we perform and excludes tenant damage and normal wear.

faqs.q: Do you renovate rentals in Pflugerville, Round Rock and Manor?
faqs.a: Yes. Much of the Austin-area rental stock sits in suburbs such as Pflugerville, Round Rock, Hutto, Manor, Leander, Kyle and Buda, often in subdivisions with active homeowners associations. We confirm the building department and HOA rules for each address, then apply your portfolio standard so finishes and reporting stay consistent. HOA approvals for exterior work are requested early so they do not hold up a turn.

faqs.q: How do you handle asbestos in older Austin rentals?
faqs.a: Many postwar Austin homes contain asbestos in siding, floor tile, mastic, ceiling texture or duct wrap. We test suspect materials before disturbing them, and where asbestos is present we coordinate licensed abatement or leave intact materials undisturbed and encapsulated when that is the safer and more practical option. Lead-safe practices apply to painted surfaces in homes built before 1978.

faqs.q: Can a renovation help my rental avoid code problems?
faqs.a: Yes. Austin Code enforces maintenance standards on rental properties, and repeated violations can bring a property into the Repeat Offender Program. We build scopes around the items code officers check most, including smoke alarms, egress, electrical safety, plumbing, stairs and railings and exterior maintenance, and document the work so you have records if questions arise later.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & Fourplex Renovation in Austin, TX | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Austin 2–4 unit renovations: 1980s side-by-side duplexes, Hyde Park and North Loop fourplexes, and HOME-era added units, phased around tenants and permits.
multifamily-renovation.intro: Austin has an unusual stock of small multifamily buildings. During the 1980s, builders put up large numbers of side-by-side duplexes on single-family lots across South Austin, North Central Austin and the areas near the university, and many of them are now worn but well located. Older neighborhoods like Hyde Park, North Loop and Travis Heights also contain fourplexes and converted houses from the 1940s through the 1970s. And since the HOME initiative, more lots are being rebuilt or expanded to hold two or three units. Genstone helps investors renovate duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes across Austin by coordinating licensed local contractors, phasing work around tenants and managing permits through Development Services. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work before you buy, so you can test it against rents and the refinance.

sections.body:
The classic Austin duplex is a two-unit building from the late 1970s or 1980s, often mirror-image units sharing a central wall, with small kitchens, one or two baths per side and a shared parking area. They sit on slabs, many on clay soils that have moved over the decades. Common problems include foundation movement, aluminum branch wiring in some buildings, polybutylene supply lines in some, original windows and sliding doors, aging HVAC, worn roofs and tired interiors after years of student or short-term tenants.

Our scopes for these buildings start with a foundation evaluation and a check of wiring and supply lines, because those determine both safety and appraisal. Then we update kitchens and baths, replace flooring with waterproof vinyl plank, upgrade windows and HVAC for efficiency and improve exterior drainage. We also look at the party wall between units for fire separation and sound transmission, which affects tenant satisfaction more than most finishes. Because these buildings are usually mirror images, ordering materials for both sides together keeps costs and schedules tighter.

sections.h2: Older fourplexes and converted houses in central Austin
sections.body:
In Hyde Park, North Loop, Travis Heights and the neighborhoods around UT, small apartment buildings and converted houses date from the 1940s through the 1970s. They often have undersized electrical service, shared water heaters, galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains, and some still have window units rather than central systems. Converted houses may have limited fire separation between units and egress issues from upper floors.

We start by inventorying each unit's systems and identifying shared ones, then scope electrical service upgrades, separate metering where practical, plumbing replacement, individual HVAC, improved fire separation and smoke detection and safe egress. Many of these properties sit in or near local historic districts or fall under residential design standards, so exterior work is planned with review in mind. Tree protections on mature central lots can also affect where new utility lines run. Because these buildings are often fully occupied, we phase the work unit by unit, schedule shared shutoffs with written notice and keep common areas safe throughout the project.

sections.h2: Added units, HOME rules and permits
sections.body:
The HOME initiative changed the math on many Austin lots by allowing additional units on most single-family parcels. Investors now buy a house, renovate it, and add a second or third unit, or convert an existing garage or accessory structure into a legal dwelling. That approach can raise income substantially, but it turns a renovation into a mix of rehab and new construction, with separate review for setbacks, impervious cover, utilities, tree protection and fire access.

Permits for renovation and new units go through the City of Austin Development Services Department, and trade permits must be pulled by licensed contractors. Water and wastewater capacity from Austin Water and electrical service from Austin Energy need to be confirmed for each new unit. We price the renovation of the existing building, help you understand the site constraints that will drive the design for an added unit and coordinate the work so the existing tenants are disturbed as little as possible. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review is the right place to see whether the lot supports the plan before you buy.

faqs.q: Can I convert an Austin garage into a rental unit?
faqs.a: Often, yes, under the HOME rules and the city's accessory dwelling provisions, but the structure must meet current code for framing, insulation, egress, fire separation and utilities, and setbacks and impervious cover limits still apply. We evaluate the existing building and price the conversion, including new water, sewer and electrical connections, so you can compare it against building a new unit.

faqs.q: What do 1980s Austin duplexes usually need?
faqs.a: Expect a foundation evaluation, a check for aluminum branch wiring and polybutylene supply lines, updated kitchens and baths, new flooring, windows and HVAC, and better drainage around the slab. The party wall between units is also worth attention for fire separation and sound. We order materials for both units together to keep costs and schedules efficient.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a fourplex while tenants live there?
faqs.a: Yes. We start with vacant units, then move through occupied ones as leases end or tenants relocate into finished units. Shared shutoffs are announced in writing in advance and kept short, and common areas stay safe and clean. Our field manager coordinates access and keeps you updated so you can communicate with tenants clearly throughout the project.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Austin, TX | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor in Austin: midcentury ranch updates, foundation repair, asbestos abatement and efficiency work bid for Limited or Standard loans.
fha-203k.intro: For Austin buyers, an FHA 203(k) loan can turn a dated midcentury ranch in Windsor Park or Crestview into an affordable path into a central neighborhood. The loan combines the purchase price and the repair budget into one mortgage, and the work is completed after closing with funds released in draws. That matters in Austin, where many lower-priced listings need exactly what conventional financing will not tolerate: foundation movement, asbestos siding, original wiring, failing HVAC or a roof at the end of its life. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, and we work with buyers, agents, lenders and HUD consultants across Austin to produce the line-item bids and draw schedules the program requires, then coordinate licensed local contractors to complete the work. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps buyers see likely repair costs before writing an offer.

sections.h2: Limited and Standard on Austin houses
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) handles non-structural work up to $75,000 and does not require a HUD consultant. In Austin it suits houses with a sound foundation that need practical updates: a new roof, HVAC replacement, insulation and duct sealing, an electrical panel upgrade, new windows, flooring, paint and a kitchen or bath refresh. Many 1970s and 1980s houses in South Austin and the Rundberg area fit this profile, as do postwar ranches whose foundations check out.

The Standard 203(k) is required when the scope includes structural work. In Austin, that usually means foundation repair on clay east of MoPac, removing a load-bearing wall to open a ranch kitchen, or rebuilding a failing addition. Standard loans require at least $5,000 in repairs and a HUD consultant who inspects the property, prepares the write-up and approves each draw. We work with the consultant from the first visit so our bid lines up with the write-up and foundation work is sequenced before drywall and paint.

sections.h2: Austin homes that fit the program well
sections.body:
The best Austin 203(k) candidates are houses in neighborhoods buyers want, held back by problems that are visible and fixable. A 1950s ranch in Windsor Park or Highland with original windows, asbestos siding, an old panel and a tired kitchen can become a comfortable, efficient home through a Limited or Standard loan, depending on the foundation. A 1980s house in Dove Springs or Southpark Meadows with aging HVAC, worn flooring and an old roof is a straightforward Limited project.

Austin adds a few local considerations. Asbestos testing and abatement may be needed before siding or flooring is removed, and lead-safe practices apply to older paint. Unpermitted garage conversions or additions may need to be legalized or reversed for the loan to close. In historic districts like Hyde Park, exterior changes need review. Work near protected trees may require special methods. We identify these items during the early estimate so buyers, agents and lenders can plan with full information.

sections.h2: How bids and draws work on an Austin 203(k)
sections.body:
A 203(k) moves on documentation. Lenders need a contractor bid broken out by line item with labor and materials, and on a Standard loan the bid must match the consultant's write-up. After closing, repair funds are held and released in draws as work is completed and inspected. Projects above the $15,000 threshold carry additional inspection and documentation requirements.

Genstone's estimators prepare bids in the format Austin lenders and consultants expect, and our field manager coordinates draw inspections as each phase finishes. We do not ask for upfront payment and tie draws to completed work, which matches how the program releases funds. Permits are pulled through the City of Austin Development Services Department or the relevant suburban building office, and sign-offs accompany each draw request. Because many buyers are paying rent while work happens, we order long-lead items like HVAC equipment and windows promptly after closing and schedule efficiency work so the home is comfortable from move-in day.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) pay for asbestos siding removal in Austin?
faqs.a: Yes. Abatement of asbestos-containing materials can be included as an eligible repair, and it is common on postwar Austin ranches with cement-asbestos shingle siding. We arrange testing, include licensed abatement and replacement siding in the bid, and schedule abatement before other exterior work begins so the project stays safe and compliant.

faqs.q: Does a 203(k) cover energy improvements?
faqs.a: Yes. Insulation, duct sealing, high-efficiency HVAC, new windows and similar improvements are eligible repairs. In Austin, these upgrades lower utility bills and improve comfort through long summers, and they often make sense to include alongside other repairs. We price them as separate line items so buyers and lenders can see the cost of each improvement.

faqs.q: Do you work with Austin agents and loan officers?
faqs.a: Yes. Agents and loan officers often ask us to walk a listing with the buyer early, so the repair estimate is realistic before the offer is final. We then prepare the line-item bid, coordinate with the HUD consultant on Standard loans and keep everyone updated as draws are requested, inspected and released.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Austin, TX | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Austin REO renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs: freeze and ice-storm damage, creek flooding, mold, vandalism and Austin Code compliance, documented.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Austin
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned homes in Austin often come with damage from the weather events that defined recent years: pipes split during Winter Storm Uri, roofs punctured by limbs in the 2023 ice storm, and, near Onion, Williamson and Walnut creeks, flood history. Add the usual problems of vacancy, such as mold from a shut-off air conditioner, stolen condensers and copper, broken windows and overgrown yards that draw Austin Code complaints, and the asset can lose value quickly. Genstone works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, which use us as a preferred contractor, to stabilize and renovate REO properties across the Austin metro. Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, inspections and code compliance, while our construction team handles repairs, all coordinated through licensed local contractors and documented for asset managers.

sections.h2: What vacant Austin houses tend to need
sections.body:
Freeze and ice damage are recurring themes in Austin REO properties. Winter Storm Uri burst pipes in attics and exterior walls across the city, and vacant homes without heat or winterization were among the hardest hit. The 2023 ice storm brought down limbs from mature oaks and pecans onto roofs, gutters and fences, and some damage went unrepaired while homes sat in foreclosure. Roof leaks that ran for months leave stained ceilings, wet insulation and mold.

Flood history is another factor near creeks. Some neighborhoods along Onion Creek saw buyouts after major floods, and other creekside homes have been through water more than once. We check for signs of past flooding and confirm floodplain status before scoping. Vacancy adds the usual problems: mold where the air conditioning was off through a humid summer, stolen AC condensers, water heaters and copper, broken windows and overgrown lots. Foundation movement on clay soils can worsen without irrigation. Our initial inspection documents each condition with photos so servicers can decide quickly between repair and as-is disposition.

sections.h2: Repair scopes matched to Austin buyers
sections.body:
Austin REO properties typically move through stabilization, repair and listing preparation. Stabilization includes securing the property, winterizing plumbing, tarping roofs, removing fallen limbs, trash-outs and addressing immediate hazards, much of it handled by Genstone Field Services. Repairs focus on items that affect value or financing, such as roof replacement, plumbing repairs, mold remediation, HVAC replacement and foundation work. Listing preparation covers paint, flooring, cleaning and curb appeal.

The right level of repair depends heavily on location. In central and east Austin, a buyer may value the lot more than the house, and a light scope for an as-is sale can make sense. In outer neighborhoods and suburbs, owner-occupant buyers using FHA financing are often the strongest market, which calls for a scope that meets minimum property requirements. Our estimators can price both options so asset managers can compare likely net proceeds. Debris removal is included in every estimate, and draws are tied to completed, documented work.

Austin Code enforces property maintenance standards on vacant homes, including tall grass and weeds, open structures, accumulated trash and unsafe conditions. Serious cases can be referred to the city's Building and Standards Commission. Genstone Field Services monitors properties on a schedule, maintains yards and responds to code notices quickly so violations do not accumulate while the asset is marketed.

When repair work begins, permits go through the City of Austin Development Services Department, or through the building office of suburban cities like Pflugerville, Round Rock or Manor, or Travis or Williamson County for unincorporated addresses. Work in floodplains may face additional review, and tree protections can affect repairs on mature lots. Lien waivers and contractor compliance documentation are collected on every job, and inspection sign-offs are kept with the project file so buyers' agents and lenders can see exactly what was repaired and permitted.

faqs.q: Do you handle tree damage on Austin REO properties?
faqs.a: Yes. After ice storms and high winds, fallen limbs often damage roofs, gutters and fences on vacant homes. We coordinate tree removal, roof and gutter repair and debris haul-off, and we trim limbs that still threaten the roof. Where protected trees are involved, we follow city requirements so the work does not create a new compliance problem.

faqs.q: Can you assess flood-damaged REO homes near Austin creeks?
faqs.a: Yes. We inspect for water lines, damaged drywall and insulation, mold and foundation issues, confirm floodplain status and review whether earlier repairs were permitted. That information helps servicers decide whether to repair, sell as-is or pursue another disposition, and it supports accurate disclosures to buyers.

faqs.q: Do you work on REO properties in Austin suburbs?
faqs.a: Yes. Our licensed contractor network covers Austin and nearby cities including Pflugerville, Round Rock, Manor, Cedar Park, Leander, Kyle and Buda, plus unincorporated Travis and Williamson counties. Each property gets a field manager and the same documentation format, and we confirm the correct permit office and any HOA rules for each address.
